title: Setup words
teaches: The names on our setup list and what each one means: the Kicker, Oops Reversal, Slingshot, Launchpad, High Volume Edge (HVC), Gap Support and the Go Signal, the catalog family each sits in, the Bear gap lesson, and the plan words every setup carries: trigger, stop, R, the first sell as a judgment (usually day 3 or later), the stop to breakeven, partials, trail.

walkthroughs.title: Every setup carries a plan
steps: Every setup we teach hands you two prices before you buy: the trigger, which is your entry, and the stop.
R is your risk per share, entry to stop. The first sell is judgment, usually day 3 or later.
Sell into a push, trail the rest. The stop follows it up under each higher low, or the 9 or 20 EMA.

walkthroughs.title: Names and families
steps: There are a lot of names. Sort them into families and they're easier to keep straight.
Gaps & Catalysts: the Kicker, the High Volume Edge and Gap Support.
Reversals & Reclaims: the Oops Reversal and the Slingshot. Bases & Breakouts: the Launchpad.
Intraday: the Go Signal and the ORB, the opening range break.

walkthroughs.title: A name is not an edge
steps: The textbook kicker: a red candle, then a gap up the other way.
Some guides call it highly reliable. Bulkowski tested it. It reversed the trend 53% of the time. Basically a coin flip.
So I don't trade the name. I trade the plan: the trigger, the stop, and a first sell by judgment.

questions.q: Every setup plan hands you two prices before you trade. One is the stop. What's the trigger?
choices: The price where you get in
The price that says you're wrong
questions.answer: The price where you get in
questions.why: The price where you get in. Trigger means entry. Every plan we teach gives you two prices, the trigger and the stop. When the stock trades through the trigger, you buy at market. You don't buy before it, and you don't wait for the close. The stop is the other price, the one that tells you you're wrong. Selling comes later, and the first sell is a judgment call.
questions.lesson_line: Trigger means entry. Price trades through it, you're in.

wrong.The price that says you're wrong: That's the stop. You need both prices, but the trigger is where you get in.
wrong.Your first profit target: Selling comes later, and the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed target.
wrong.The headline that moved it: News can be why a stock moves. The trigger is a price on the chart.

questions.simple: The trigger is your entry. When price trades through it, you buy.

reasons: wrong note rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, E51)
fixed before

questions.lesson_line: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. Every trade plan we teach runs in that order.
questions.simple: Trim comes third because you take some profit off as the trade works, then trail the rest.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A12, E51)

questions.q: Someone in chat says a stock on your list just printed a bullish kicker. What do the last two daily candles look like?
choices: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
A green candle, then a gap-down red one
One candle with a long lower wick
A small candle inside the prior range
questions.answer: A red candle, then a gap-up green one
questions.why: A red candle, then a green one that gaps up. That's the flip. One day sellers are in charge and it closes weak. The next morning it opens up and away from that red day. The mirror, a green day and then a gap-down red one, is the bearish kicker. You always need two candles with a gap between them. One candle alone, however long its wick, isn't a kicker.
questions.lesson_line: Kicker: a down day, then a gap up the other way. Two candles, one gap.

wrong.A green candle, then a gap-down red one: That's the bearish kicker, the mirror image. You're looking for the bullish one.
wrong.One candle with a long lower wick: One candle can't be a kicker. It takes two candles with a gap between them.
wrong.A small candle inside the prior range: That's an inside day. It has no gap, and a kicker gaps away from the day before.

questions.simple: A red day, then a green day that gaps up above it. Two candles, a gap between them.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree; stable definition

deeper.example: Investopedia: bullish kickers start with a bearish candle and then show a bullish gap up. Bulkowski's version is stricter. He wants a tall black marubozu, an upward gap, then a tall white marubozu.

questions.q: You hear someone on our desk call a stock an Oops. What just happened on its chart?
choices: Lost yesterday's close, took it back
Gapped up the day after a red day
Broke out of a tight MA squeeze
questions.answer: Lost yesterday's close, took it back
questions.why: It lost yesterday's close and took it back the same day. That's the Oops. Sellers push it under the prior close and people bail. Then buyers take the level back, and those sellers are caught on the wrong side. The reclaim of yesterday's close is your trigger. Your stop goes under the low of the day, the LOD. The first sell is a judgment, and the rest trails under each higher low.
questions.lesson_line: Oops: it lost the prior close and took it back the same day.

wrong.Gapped up the day after a red day: That's the Kicker, a red day and then a gap up the next morning.
wrong.Back over the 4-day high line: That's the Slingshot, price trading back over the 4-day average of the highs.
wrong.Broke out of a tight MA squeeze: That's the Launchpad, price breaking out of a squeeze of moving averages.

questions.simple: The stock dropped under yesterday's close, then climbed back over it the same day. The reclaim is your entry.

reasons: house definition from TRADE_PLANS.md; stable

questions.q: What does a Launchpad look like on the daily chart?
choices: Price breaking out of a tight MA squeeze
Back over the 4-day average of highs
A pullback that holds an old gap
A weak open that buyers turn up
questions.answer: Price breaking out of a tight MA squeeze
questions.why: Price breaking out of a tight squeeze of moving averages. The 20 EMA and 50 SMA come together, price sits right on top of them, and the range goes quiet. That squeeze is stored energy. When price trades up and out of it, you buy at market, never at the close. I'd put the stop under the low of the day first. The app also draws a line stop a quarter ATR under the lower average.
questions.lesson_line: Launchpad: the averages squeeze together, then price launches out of it.

wrong.A weak open that buyers turn up: That's the Go Signal, a strong stock that opens weak and gets turned.
wrong.A pullback that holds an old gap: That's Gap Support, a pullback that holds an old gap.
wrong.Back over the 4-day average of highs: That's the Slingshot. Its line is a short average of the highs, not a squeeze of averages.

questions.simple: A Launchpad is moving averages squeezed tight, then price breaking up and out of the squeeze.

reasons: house definition from TRADE_PLANS.md; stable

questions.q: You tell a friend you're trading Gap Support today. What are you actually doing?
choices: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
Shorting a gap down off the highs
Buying the open of any gap up
Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying
questions.answer: Buying a pullback that holds a gap
questions.why: Buying a pullback that holds a gap. The stock gaps up and runs. Later it comes back to the gap, and the gap holds. That gap is where buyers stepped in hard, so it's a clean line to lean on. You buy as it trades up through the trigger while the gap holds. Your stop goes under the gap top or the low of the day, whichever is lower.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support: the gap holds, you buy, and the gap is your line.

wrong.Shorting a gap down off the highs: Gap Support is a long. A gap down off the highs is our Bear gap lesson, and that one is studied, not traded.
wrong.Buying the open of any gap up: That's chasing the gap. Gap Support waits for the pullback and for the gap to prove it holds.
wrong.Waiting for a gap to fill, then buying: A filled gap has failed as support. We buy while the gap still holds.

questions.simple: You buy a stock that pulled back to an old gap up and is holding it.

reasons: fixed before

questions.q: We mark the HVC on every High Volume Edge chart. What is that level?
choices: The close of a high-volume day
The highest price of the day
A high-volume gap at the open
questions.answer: The close of a high-volume day
questions.why: The close of the high-volume day. HVC stands for High Volume Close. When a stock trades far more shares than it has in a long time, big money was busy that day. Where it closed is a price those buyers care about. So we mark it and watch how price acts when it comes back. The buy still comes as price trades through a trigger, never at the close.
questions.lesson_line: HVC: where the heavy-volume day closed. Mark it, then watch the retest.

wrong.The highest price of the day: That's the day's high. The HVC is where the heavy-volume day closed.
wrong.A high-volume gap at the open: It's not about the open or a gap. The HVC is the close of that heavy day.
wrong.Volume above its 50-day average: That's a volume reading, not a price. The HVC is a price you can mark on the chart.

questions.simple: The HVC is the close of a huge-volume day, a price we mark and watch.

reasons: the HVC expansion has no citable house quote (owner flag)

questions.q: What does our Go Signal look like while it's happening?
choices: A weak open that buyers turn back up
A gap up the day after a red day
A pullback that holds an older gap up
A break out of a tight MA cluster
questions.answer: A weak open that buyers turn back up
questions.why: A weak open that buyers turn back up. It's a strong stock, one that has already shown it can move. This morning it opens under yesterday's close and flushes a nearby support. The weak hands sell. Then buyers step in and turn it. You want the turn, not the flush. questions.q: You're writing the plan for a new trade. In what order do the pieces go?
questions.why: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. First where you get in, then where you're wrong. Then where you take some off, and how you ride what's left. The stop comes before any profit, because it's your plan for when you're wrong. The trim itself is a judgment, and we very rarely sell on day 1.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. Every plan runs in that order.

wrong.Entry, Trim, Stop, Trail: The stop goes in before any profit is taken. It's the plan for when the trade turns.
wrong.Stop, Entry, Trail, Trim: A stop protects a position, so you need the entry first.
wrong.Entry, Stop, Trail, Trim: You trim first, then trail what's left. The trail rides the part you kept.

questions.simple: Entry, Stop, Trim, Trail. Get in, set your stop, take some off, then trail the rest.

questions.q: Your stock is up 4R and still acting great. What's the play?
choices: Sell partials, trail the rising averages
Sell the whole position at the first pop
Hold the full size until the stop hits
Move the stop down to give it room
questions.answer: Sell partials, trail the rising averages
questions.why: Sell some into strength and trail the rest. Selling partials banks part of the gain, so a reversal can't take it all back. The rest stays on with the stop trailing the rising averages, so you're still in if it runs. Sell it all at the first pop and you miss the big leg. Hold full size to the stop and you give a lot back.
questions.lesson_line: Sell partials into strength. Trail the rest.

wrong.Sell the whole position at the first pop: Selling it all at the first pop leaves the rest of the move behind.
wrong.Hold the full size until the stop hits: Holding the full size gives a lot back if the stock turns. Sell some into strength.
wrong.Move the stop down to give it room: Moving the stop down adds risk. The stop trails up behind the rising averages.

questions.simple: Sell partials into strength and trail the rest. You bank some and keep riding the winner.

questions.q: Where does our Gap Support stop go?
choices: The lower of the gap top and day's low
The higher of the gap top and day's low
The closer of the gap top and day's low
A few cents under the prior day's close
questions.answer: The lower of the gap top and day's low
questions.why: The lower of the gap top and the day's low. Our Gap Support buys the close as the gap holds. If the trade drifts sideways at the gap, the stop tightens to just under the gap top. Our rulebook puts the stop order a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
questions.lesson_line: Gap Support stop: the lower of the gap top and the day's low.

wrong.The higher of the gap top and day's low: Our card says whichever is lower, not higher.
wrong.The closer of the gap top and day's low: Whichever is closer is the Kicker's rule. Gap Support takes whichever is lower.
wrong.A few cents under the prior day's close: Our Gap Support stop is tied to the gap top and the day's low, not the prior close.

questions.simple: The lower of the gap top and the day's low, because our Gap Support stop goes on whichever sits further down.

This unit follows TRADE_PLANS.md only and never uses lesson_key slugs or the older glossary as a source. The owner may want the old glossary items retired.

Kicker: the textbook shape is narrower than our detector. Investopedia's bullish kicker opens at or beyond the first candle's open; Bulkowski's bullish kicking is two marubozu candles with an upward gap. Our uct_kicker detector fires on a weak prior close, an open above the prior close and a trade through the prior high. The unit teaches the shape 'in candle terms' (q03, from two Tier 2 publishers) and our plan from TRADE_PLANS.md; it never says our Kicker needs marubozu candles. q28's story fits both (it opens above the red day's open and trades through its high).

Kicker reliability: Investopedia calls kickers 'rare but highly reliable'; Bulkowski measured the bullish kicking at 53% ('almost random'). Asked only as what each source says (q51, w3), never as a prediction.

Opening range window: Investopedia defines the opening range on the first 15 minutes and notes day traders often use the first half hour. Our Kicker ORB is the 30-minute range (the owner's ruling). q55 asks it as ours.

Gap definition: Investopedia (breakaway gap page) measures a gap from the prior close to the open; Bulkowski requires today's low above yesterday's high. No question here quizzes a general gap definition; Gap Support's 'gap top' and the Bear gap line are taken from TRADE_PLANS.md.

Oops Reversal: Larry Williams's classic Oops (open below the prior day's low, then a buy back at that low) differs from ours (the prior close, reclaimed during the day; the detector also wants an undercut of the prior low). No reliable page for Williams's version could be read (definitions.json records a 403 on the magazine article; this session's web search budget ran out), so only our version is taught.

High Volume Edge on a down close: TRADE_PLANS.md gives the stop as 'its high on a down close' (the detector reads a down-close edge bar as bearish). q24 asks only what the stop is, not how to trade the short side.

The Oops Reversal and the Go Signal share the same entry mechanic (the prior close, reclaimed in the session). TRADE_PLANS.md lists the Go Signal's checks but not the Oops's, so no question says what one needs that the other does not, and no question offers both as choices where both would fit.

HVC: skill_map.json lists HVC only as an alias of the High Volume Edge. q07 reads it as the high-volume close from TRADE_PLANS.md's entry wording; the detector's docstring (uct_hve.py, not a citable source) says the same: 'the high-volume close (HVC)'.

Gap top: TRADE_PLANS.md uses 'the gap top' without defining it (uct_gap_support.py takes it as the prior day's high, the top of the range before the gap). No question asks what the gap top is; questions give it as a price.

R and the trims: until 2026-11-09 TRADE_PLANS.md put the detectors' targets 'at 2R and 3R from that stop' and named no fraction; the owner's account rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9, B19, E51) replaces it with a third at 3R (stop to breakeven), a third at 5R, the last third trailed, and TRADE_PLANS.md was rewritten to match.
